Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Situation2: They notice a minor ethical dilemma at work, like someone cutting in line, and feel a mild urge to act.
Story:
It was already past midnight when my phone buzzed. My friend’s voice trembled through the speaker—her car had broken down on the highway, and she was alone, scared, and desperate for help. As her friend, I knew what was expected of me: to drop everything and rush to her side, no matter the hour. I grabbed my keys, heart pounding, ready to go.

But as I hurried through the lobby of my apartment building, I saw a coworker quietly slip ahead of an elderly woman in the queue for the night security check. As a Hindu, I was raised to value dharma—righteousness and fairness in all actions, no matter how small. My conscience screamed at me to speak up, to gently remind my coworker of what was right. Yet, my friend’s voice echoed in my mind, pleading for help.

I stood frozen, torn between the urgent call of friendship and the quiet but insistent tug of my moral duty. My hands shook as I weighed the demands of both roles, feeling the pressure of two worlds colliding inside me.
